overview: I study how organizations design and operate systems whose decisions are coupled across resources, locations and time. The central challenge is to connect local choices with their consequences elsewhere. Purchasing decisions affect production and inventory; infrastructure investment determines future operating options; disruptions alter both the available resources and the commitments they must support.

My research combines mathematical modeling with algorithm design to examine these dependencies. Published studies in logistics and infrastructure planning provide a foundation for broader questions about coordination, adaptation and technological change. My long-term interests span operations and supply chain management, public-service systems, and the interaction between artificial intelligence and mathematical optimization.

algorithms.question: How can the structure of interdependent decisions inform more effective optimization and learning methods?
paragraphs: My methodological interests concern the relationship between a mathematical representation and the computation it makes possible. I study how assignment, sequencing and resource dependencies can be represented compactly, and how their structure supports decomposition and exact improvement. These questions arise across scheduling and allocation problems, rather than within a single application. My published berth-scheduling and cross-docking studies provide concrete settings for developing and comparing such methods.

A complementary line studies how computation should adapt during search. Hyperheuristics select operators according to their observed performance, while exact subproblem optimization improves or evaluates candidate schedules. The important question is how these components interact under a finite time budget. Feasibility, solution quality, bounds and time to a usable schedule provide different evidence about an algorithm’s performance.

A longer-term interest is learning across the optimization process. Learned policies might guide repeated decisions, while language models could assist with formulation, scenario construction or the interpretation of results. The research challenge is to connect these capabilities with mathematical checks and useful solver feedback. I am interested in their performance on unfamiliar problems, the cost of adaptation, and the conditions under which a manager should retain or revise an analytical recommendation.
questions: Which dependencies must be represented explicitly, and which admit decomposition without losing feasibility or useful bounds?
How should computation be allocated between adaptive exploration and exact improvement?
Under what conditions do learned strategies transfer across problem instances, and how should solver feedback guide AI-generated models and algorithms?

maritime.question: When does coordination create greater value than additional capacity, and how should that value be shared?
paragraphs: I am interested in how operations should be coordinated across stages, facilities and organizations. Local efficiency can coexist with poor system performance when arrivals, processing, inventory and departures are planned independently. Mathematical models can reveal which decisions require joint treatment and where decomposition preserves the essential interactions. My work in berth scheduling and cross-docking examines these dependencies through shared capacity, service precedence and timing.

The broader research question concerns coordination across facilities and organizations. I plan to study sourcing, production, inventory and distribution decisions under different arrangements for information sharing and decision authority. Comparisons between joint and decentralized planning can identify where coordination creates value, which constraints limit that value, and how gains are distributed. Incentives matter when participants bear different costs or disruption risks.

Product characteristics can change the coordination problem as much as facility capacity. My collaborative pharmaceutical-supply-chain review separates medicine distribution from reverse collection, sorting, recovery, recycling and disposal. Its content analysis and conceptual framework connect planning decisions with cold-chain requirements, resilience and sustainability. This work motivates broader interests in coordinating material flows across an entire product lifecycle, including systems with perishability and limited recovery options.
questions: How do upstream and downstream dependencies change bottlenecks and the value of processing, storage or transport capacity?
How do information sharing, contractual commitments and decision authority affect coordination and the distribution of benefits?
How should technology adoption and supporting infrastructure be planned alongside the operating policies that determine their value?

resilience.question: How should systems invest in flexibility and adapt operating commitments when disruption changes what is feasible?
paragraphs: My interests in resilience connect system design with adaptation during operations. Supplier alternatives, reserve capacity and inventory buffers create options whose value depends on when and how they can be used. I plan to examine how those options should be distributed across a network and coordinated with recovery policies. Published ship-schedule recovery studies provide an initial setting for analyzing competing service, economic and environmental objectives.

Electrification connects investment choices with daily schedules. My collaborative review of electric-vehicle scheduling distinguishes general operating constraints from power-grid and environmental considerations, with representative models for each category. Related electric-tugboat research combines literature analysis, industry interviews and economic assessment. Together, these studies motivate questions about charging capacity, utilization and financing that cannot be answered from equipment specifications alone.

Healthcare and humanitarian operations introduce additional priorities into resource allocation. Scarce capacity may need to support urgent demand, continuity of service and geographic access at the same time. My interests include rolling planning, the cost of revising commitments and the allocation of computational effort under tight deadlines. Proposed methods would be assessed through feasible service plans and explicit trade-offs, rather than a single aggregate efficiency measure.
questions: How should reserve capacity, inventory and alternative resources be positioned when their value depends on the recovery policy?
Which commitments should be protected or revised as disruption information changes?
How can allocation models evaluate service and access together with energy, environmental and economic consequences?

cases.title: Compact formulations and decomposition for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A compact berth-scheduling formulation supports Benders decomposition and column generation for larger planning problems.
cases.question: How does formulation design affect the scalability of exact berth-scheduling optimization?
cases.approach: The study minimizes total vessel service costs in dynamic, discrete berth scheduling. Two-dimensional decision variables, the removal of redundant model elements and simplified sequencing reduce the size of the mixed-integer formulation. Benders decomposition and column generation exploit the resulting structure to address larger scheduling instances.
cases.evidence: The computational study compares the formulation with five mathematical models and three metaheuristics. It reports solutions for instances with more than 260 vessels within two hours under the tested settings, alongside sensitivity analysis of operational parameters.
cases.meaning: The formulation illustrates how modeling choices affect the scale at which exact optimization can be applied. Its reduced representation also supports decomposition, linking formulation design to the development of solution methods.
cases.connection: The formulation and decomposition ideas may also apply to problems that combine resource assignments with sequencing.
cases.futureQuestion: How can compact formulations be extended to coordinated resource decisions when berthing, handling and downstream service interact?

cases.title: Integrated truck scheduling and freight-transfer coordination
cases.summary: Sequential optimization and pricing-guided search address coupled truck services, freight transfers and departure timing.
cases.question: How should freight transfers, handling capacity and service precedence be represented in integrated truck schedules?
cases.approach: The mixed-integer model coordinates dock assignments, service sequences and timing across inbound unloading, freight transfer and outbound loading. It accounts for waiting, handling, temporary storage and departure-delay costs. Sequential fix-and-optimize constructs precedence-consistent batches. Pricing-guided search uses reduced-cost information to identify promising single-truck reinsertions, with exact evaluation after discrete scheduling decisions are fixed.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments compare the model and both solution frameworks. Sensitivity analyses examine how scheduling parameters affect costs and operations.
cases.meaning: The contribution concerns both representation and computation. Freight-transfer precedence and shared handling capacity must remain consistent when a truck is moved within a schedule. The two frameworks exploit that structure differently, through staged construction and targeted neighborhood improvement. Their computational evaluation explains when larger integrated plans can be obtained within a practical planning budget.
cases.connection: This work motivates my interest in coordinating schedules across processing, transfer and service stages.
cases.futureQuestion: When should additional processing or storage capacity be preferred to improved coordination of inbound and outbound operations?

cases.title: Thompson Sampling for adaptive scheduling heuristics
cases.summary: Thompson Sampling adapts operator selection while repair and exact evaluation address schedule feasibility and accuracy.
cases.question: How can adaptive operator selection improve search while preserving reliable schedule evaluation?
cases.approach: The Hybridized Thompson Sampling Hyperheuristic combines evolutionary search with an adaptive operator-selection controller. A repair-and-penalty mechanism handles inbound–outbound precedence constraints. Fast approximate fitness evaluation supports exploration, while exact optimization refines schedule evaluation.
cases.evidence: On the reported benchmark instances, the algorithm produces solutions comparable with exact optimization for small problems and improves on the comparison metaheuristics. The paper reports improvements of up to approximately 24% and an average runtime of 186.71 seconds across its experimental setting.
cases.meaning: This study treats operator selection, constraint handling and schedule evaluation as separate design decisions within one algorithm. Thompson Sampling adapts the search operators; repair and penalties address precedence; approximate evaluation limits the cost of exploration. Exact optimization then refines evaluation. Their interaction explains the method’s computational design, beyond the label of a hybrid algorithm.
cases.connection: A next question is whether the learned search strategies remain useful under different demand patterns and operating conditions.
cases.futureQuestion: Can adaptive search strategies transfer between demand patterns and facilities while preserving feasible schedules?

cases.title: Hybrid hyperheuristics and exact optimization for berth scheduling
cases.summary: A berth-scheduling hyperheuristic adapts genetic operators and periodically applies problem-specific exact improvement.
cases.question: How can adaptive search and exact subproblem optimization complement one another in berth scheduling?
cases.approach: The Hyperheuristic Hybridized with Exact Optimization addresses dynamic, discrete berth allocation and scheduling. It chooses genetic operators according to their observed performance and periodically applies berth-specific exact optimization procedures to improve candidate schedules.
cases.evidence: Computational comparisons examine the algorithm against exact-optimization-inspired methods and established metaheuristics. Component experiments investigate the contribution of hyperheuristic control and hybridization. Scenario analysis considers berth availability, vessel arrival intensity and departure-delay penalties.
cases.meaning: The algorithm allocates computation between exploration across genetic operators and exact improvement of berth-specific schedules. Operator performance changes during search, so the controller uses observed results to revise its choices. Component experiments examine what is gained from adaptation and exact improvement within the combined procedure.
cases.connection: I am interested in how to divide computation between broad search and exact improvement in other scheduling problems.
cases.futureQuestion: How should limited computation be divided between broad search and structured exact improvement as a planning problem changes?

cases.title: Optimization for highway–rail crossing closure decisions
cases.summary: An optimization framework considers safety, economic and environmental effects alongside delay and maintenance costs.
cases.question: How should safety, economic and environmental effects enter the prioritization of rail-crossing closures?
cases.approach: The study develops an optimization model that includes safety, economic and environmental benefits as well as traffic-delay and maintenance implications. A sorting-inspired heuristic addresses the resulting decision problem. Computational experiments use crossings in Florida.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use Florida crossing data to compare the sorting-inspired heuristic with an exact method. Across the reported instances, it was approximately twenty times faster, with an average optimality gap of 0.14%. Sensitivity analyses examine how model inputs affect the selected closures.
cases.meaning: Related collaborative research extends closure selection to the allocation of crossing interventions. The 2026 study compares countermeasure installation, grade separation and closure under budget and feasibility constraints. Experiments with 5,939 publicly managed Florida crossings examine safety and socio-environmental trade-offs, including delay, emissions, noise and community disruption. Together, these studies distinguish selecting an intervention from evaluating the consequences of an intervention portfolio.
cases.connection: My interest is in infrastructure investment models that make competing consequences explicit. The related multi-objective study is listed in the publication record under DOI 10.1016/j.scs.2026.107485.
cases.futureQuestion: How can infrastructure prioritization represent uncertainty and changes in access, exposure and operating conditions?

cases.title: Ship schedule recovery under environmental policies
cases.summary: Multi-objective optimization examines the tension between schedule recovery, monetary losses and speed-reduction incentives.
cases.question: How should disruption recovery be planned when service targets conflict with environmental requirements and incentives?
cases.approach: The model balances monetary losses and port-arrival delays while representing emission-control areas and voluntary speed-reduction incentives. These policies affect the recovery options directly: faster sailing may recover time, while reduced speed can earn an incentive. Dynamic secant approximation and an epsilon-constraint method generate alternative recovery plans.
cases.evidence: Computational experiments use the South East Asia Pendulum shipping route, with sensitivity analysis exploring how different settings affect recovery choices.
cases.meaning: The study makes the conflict between recovering service and complying with environmental restrictions explicit. A separate 2023 Computers & Industrial Engineering paper develops exact Pareto optimization for late arrivals and profit loss, including speed adjustment and port skipping. The two studies examine related recovery decisions through different models and solution methods.
cases.connection: My broader interest is in recovery policies that recognize both the value and the cost of changing commitments. The two ship-recovery papers provide examples of how operational and policy constraints alter the alternatives available after disruption.
cases.futureQuestion: Which commitments should be preserved during recovery, and where does flexibility provide the greatest value before a disruption?

approach: I teach optimization as a sequence of choices about a real decision problem. Students must identify what can be decided, translate operating rules into constraints and explain how an objective represents the intended outcome. A numerical answer becomes useful only when those modeling choices can be justified.

In algorithm instruction, small examples make the search process visible before students implement larger models. Comparing exact methods, local search and population-based algorithms helps explain differences in feasibility, solution quality and computation time. Projects in scheduling and resource allocation then require students to connect those comparisons with the structure of their own problems.

Students arrive with different mathematical and programming backgrounds. Guided examples and staged project work provide support while allowing greater independence as their experience develops. I ask students to check implementations, examine sensitivity to assumptions and explain the limits of their conclusions. These habits support further research as well as professional analytical work.
teaching.mentoring: I have mentored undergraduate and master’s researchers and served as an external master’s thesis committee member. I help students narrow an initial interest into a research question, choose an appropriate model and design a computational investigation. Discussion and feedback focus on interpreting evidence and explaining limitations. As a project develops, students take increasing responsibility for technical choices and scholarly communication.

agenda.title: Learning, optimization and decision support
agenda.text: I am interested in how learning and optimization can improve one another throughout a decision process. This includes learning which parts of a problem to optimize, adapting computational effort, and translating operating rules into mathematical models. Generative AI introduces questions about model validity, the interpretation of solver feedback and the division of decision authority between analytical systems and managers. I plan to evaluate these approaches through decision quality, feasibility, computational effort and the stability of recommendations when conditions change.

agenda.title: Coordination and the organization of supply chains
agenda.text: My interests extend from integrated facility schedules to the organization of decisions across firms. Sourcing, production, inventory and distribution can be planned jointly, yet the resulting benefits and risks rarely fall on the same participants. I plan to examine how information sharing, purchasing arrangements and decision authority influence system performance and incentives to cooperate. A central question is when coordination can substitute for additional capacity, and which arrangements sustain cooperation during disruption.

agenda.title: Resilience, preparedness and adaptation
agenda.text: Resilience requires decisions before uncertainty is resolved as well as effective responses afterward. I am interested in selecting supplier alternatives, inventory buffers and reserve capacity alongside the recovery policies they enable. These choices raise questions about the location of flexibility, the cost of revising commitments and the consequences of shifting bottlenecks. Optimization and simulation can compare preparedness strategies through recovery time, service continuity and the distribution of disruption costs across a network.

agenda.title: Technology investment and sustainable operations
agenda.text: Electrification and automation change the capacity, energy requirements and economics of an operating system. My interests concern the timing and scale of adoption, the allocation of capital between equipment and supporting infrastructure, and the policies governing their use. Joint investment and operating models can examine when these technologies reinforce one another and when demand or shared resources limit their value. Relevant outcomes include lifecycle cost, service reliability, energy use, emissions and workforce requirements.

agenda.title: Healthcare, humanitarian logistics and public services
agenda.text: Essential-service systems allocate scarce resources among needs that differ in urgency, location and duration. I am interested in how capacity planning, scheduling and resource deployment can support both routine service and emergency response. Research questions concern the value of advance preparation, the revision of priorities as information changes, and trade-offs between rapid response and continuity. These problems require evaluation of delays and unmet needs across populations and locations, alongside aggregate operating performance.

currentWork.title: Integrated scheduling and resource circulation
currentWork.text: Current research investigates integrated processing, vehicle scheduling and reusable-resource circulation. A resource may remain unavailable after processing ends because it must be moved, returned or repositioned. Modeling these dependencies together allows the study of bottlenecks, completion times and energy use. The computational work examines when decomposition or selective optimization can reduce effort without removing the dependencies that determine feasibility.

currentWork.title: Planning under time and capacity constraints
currentWork.text: Ongoing work in flood response and healthcare scheduling examines decisions that must be revised as needs and available capacity change. The research considers compact formulations, rolling planning and selective reoptimization. Questions include which commitments to preserve, which resources to reassign, and where limited computation can most improve the revised plan. The comparison focuses on feasible allocation, service priorities and the operational cost of revising an existing plan.

currentWork.title: Infrastructure investment and realized use
currentWork.text: My shore-power research distinguishes infrastructure commitment, implementation readiness and realized operating use. Installed capability does not by itself determine how often vessels connect or how operations change. The work examines the records needed to characterize that progression and inform subsequent investment analysis. It connects a specific infrastructure setting with my wider interest in evaluating technology adoption through both investment and operations.

currentWork.title: Language models and operational knowledge
currentWork.text: A local research prototype retrieves passages from public transportation-agency manuals and links generated responses to source material. The research concerns the interpretation of technical requirements and the reliability of cited evidence. It also motivates a broader question: how retrieved operating rules could inform a mathematical formulation and be checked against solver feedback. The prototype remains an experimental analytical tool.

evaluation.title: Mathematical structure and feasibility
evaluation.text: A model must represent the resource, timing and precedence relationships that determine whether a plan can be carried out. I am interested in compact formulations and decompositions that reduce computational effort while retaining these relationships.

evaluation.title: Computational comparisons
evaluation.text: Algorithms need to be compared under stated computational budgets and operating conditions. Solution quality, feasibility, time to a usable plan and sensitivity to problem size provide complementary evidence; a single best objective does not describe every planning requirement.

evaluation.title: Operating consequences
evaluation.text: The purpose of a computational result is to clarify a decision. Relevant questions include how a plan changes service, resource utilization, energy use or exposure to disruption, and which assumptions determine those effects.
